title: Nduoni — the skillet
description: Ide potato and egg skillet: nduonī = nduko (potato) + onī (egg).
html:
Nduonī Ide Potato & Egg Skillet Serves 2 Inspiration / Origin Inspired by: A simple potato skillet omelette, reworked with Nigerian ingredients and stricter food-safety steps. Introduction Nduonī takes its name from potato (nduko) and egg (onī). The potato is peeled into paper-thin ribbons rather than pre-cooked, so it finishes tender at the same moment the egg sets, with onion, tomato and pepper folded through for a proper Nigerian-style breakfast — and nothing, potato or egg, is ever left raw or runny. Recipe Information Serves: 2 Preparation time: 10 minutes Cooking time: 20 minutes Total time: 30 minutes Ingredients Main 1 potato, peeled into paper-thin, near-translucent ribbons 2–3 eggs Vegetables Onion, finely diced Tomato, finely diced Red scotch bonnet pepper, finely diced Fat & Seasoning Vegetable oil Curry powder, a pinch Cheddar cheese, grated Seasoning cube, crumbled Salt and black pepper Equipment Non-stick skillet with lid Vegetable peeler or slicer Mixing bowl for the eggs Preparation 1. Peel the potato into paper-thin, near-translucent ribbons using a vegetable peeler or a mandoline. This is the step that makes the dish safe without pre-cooking the potato separately — ribbons this thin cook through in the same time the egg takes to set, so there's no raw centre left behind. 2. Dice the onion, tomato and scotch bonnet pepper. 3. Whisk the eggs with a pinch of salt and black pepper. Cooking Method 1. Heat oil in a non-stick pan over medium heat and layer the raw potato ribbons evenly across the base. Season lightly with salt and the crumbled seasoning cube. 2. Pour the whisked egg over the potato ribbons right away, tilting the pan so it settles into an even layer and coats every ribbon — the potato is not cooked ahead of time. 3. Scatter the diced onion, tomato, scotch bonnet pepper and curry powder evenly over the top. 4. Cover the pan and cook on medium-low heat until the potato ribbons are tender and the egg is completely set all the way through, with no raw potato and no runny egg left at all. Because the ribbons are so thin, this happens together rather than in two separate stages. 5. Scatter the grated cheese over the top, cover briefly again, and let it melt. 6. Fold the omelette in half, slice, and serve while it's hot. Chef's Notes Peel the potato paper-thin — this, not a separate pre-cook, is what makes the dish safe. Thick slices left raw under the egg will not cook through in time. Keep the pan covered throughout so both the potato and the egg finish together with no raw or runny centre. Dice the scotch bonnet finely and taste-test your batch first — heat levels vary a lot between peppers. Variations Smoked fish flakes folded in for extra protein Green pepper and spring onion for a fresher finish Serving Suggestions Serve hot for breakfast Good with fresh bread or a slice of ripe pawpaw on the side Appearance Golden, crisp potato base Fully set egg with melted cheese on top Bright flecks of tomato and pepper throughout Flavour Profile Savoury and cheesy Mild warmth from the curry powder and scotch bonnet pepper Comforting, home-style breakfast flavour Nutritional Highlights Good source of protein from the eggs and cheese Potato provides energy-dense carbohydrate Cultural Significance Nduonī turns a casual skillet breakfast into a proper Nigerian-style dish — sharing a table with jollof and okro soup rather than sitting apart from them — while making sure it's cooked all the way through for a safe, satisfying morning meal.
